summary: Specifies a profile for DCCP Congestion Control ID 4, an experimental variant using TFRC-SP, which suits applications sending small packets. CCID 4 is for experimental use.

plainLanguage.summary: This memo defines CCID 4, an experimental congestion-control profile for DCCP. It adjusts a TCP-friendly rate calculation for small packets and adds feedback about packet losses.

questions: what is the dccp dropped packets option
how does ccid 4 differ from ccid 3
subtitle: An experimental DCCP congestion-control profile for applications that send small packets.

tldr.problem: Applications sending small packets may want a TCP-friendly rate without abrupt rate changes, but packet overhead must be included when calculating a fair rate.
tldr.mechanism: CCID 4 applies the small-packet variant of TCP-Friendly Rate Control (TFRC-SP) to DCCP and adds feedback for the number of packets lost or marked in short loss intervals.
tldr.outcome: CCID 4 is Experimental because TFRC-SP is Experimental and was not proposed for widespread Internet deployment. The unit metadata lists updates by RFC 6323 and RFC 8311.

today: RFC 5622 is an Experimental RFC published in August 2009 and was updated by RFC 6323 and RFC 8311. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes it.

sections.title: CCID 4 and Small-Packet Rate Control
sections.content:
CCID 4 is a profile for Congestion Control Identifier 4 in the Datagram Congestion Control Protocol (DCCP). It is a modified version of CCID 3 and uses TFRC-SP, an experimental small-packet variant of TCP-Friendly Rate Control (TFRC). Its goal is roughly the same bit rate as a TCP flow using packets up to 1500 bytes under the same congestion level.

It is intended for senders that use a small fixed segment size or vary their segment size as the allowed rate changes. CCID 4 determines the allowed rate but does not choose the application's segment size. It aims to avoid abrupt changes in sending rate.
sections.plainLanguage: CCID 4 sets a congestion-aware sending rate for DCCP applications that use small packets. The application chooses its packet size, while CCID 4 adjusts the permitted rate.

sections.title: Rate Limits and Loss Calculation
sections.content:
CCID 4 uses TFRC and TFRC-SP. The allowed rate is reduced to account for packet headers: the memo estimates a 36-byte header for IPv4 with 48-bit DCCP sequence numbers, or 32 bytes with 24-bit sequence numbers. For an N-byte data packet, the rate reduction factor is N/(N+36) for the stated 36-byte estimate.

The sender enforces a minimum 10 ms interval between data packets. If operating-system scheduling makes this impractical, it MAY send up to one extra packet per timeslice, provided no more than three packets are sent in any 30 ms interval. The throughput calculation uses a nominal segment size of 1460 bytes.

For loss intervals of at most two round-trip times, the loss calculation counts the packets actually lost or marked. If an interval contains N data packets and K lost or marked packets, its interval length is calculated as N/K. Longer intervals use the TFRC-SP loss-interval procedure.
sections.plainLanguage: The rate calculation accounts for the bytes used by headers, and data packets must be spaced apart. For short periods of loss, the calculation includes how many packets were lost or marked.

sections.title: Data and Feedback in a Half-Connection
sections.content:
The memo gives an informative example of one direction of a connection. The sender transmits DCCP-Data packets at the allowed rate and includes sequence numbers and a window counter. The receiver sends DCCP-Ack packets with recent loss-interval feedback, normally at least once per round-trip time unless the sender sends less than one packet during that time.

The sender uses feedback to update its rate and estimates round-trip time. If it receives no feedback within the calculated nofeedback time, which is at least four round-trip times, it halves its sending rate. A sender may calculate the loss event rate from receiver feedback or use a rate calculated by the receiver.
sections.plainLanguage: The receiver reports packet losses so the sender can adjust its rate. If feedback stops for long enough, the sender reduces its rate by half.

sections.title: Loss Feedback Options
sections.content:
CCID 4 uses the CCID 3 options and features, with a new Dropped Packets option. The Loss Intervals option reports interval lengths; the new option reports the number of packets lost or marked in each interval. Each Drop Count is a 24-bit value and MUST NOT exceed the associated Loss Length.

A Dropped Packets option can cover one to 84 consecutive loss intervals, ordered from newest to oldest. Receivers MUST include it in every feedback packet. A feedback packet with Loss Intervals must include Dropped Packets information for the same intervals. If a sender calculates the loss rate itself and the relevant Drop Count is missing, it MUST treat the count as equal to the interval's Loss Length.
sections.plainLanguage: Receiver feedback reports both the length of a loss interval and the number of packets lost or marked within it. This gives the sender the extra information it needs for short loss intervals.

sections.title: Experimental Status and Security
sections.content:
CCID 4 is considered Experimental because TFRC-SP is Experimental. RFC 4828 describes why TFRC-SP was not intended for widespread deployment in the global Internet at the time. The memo says CCID 4 should be updated if an IETF Standards Track RFC changes TFRC-SP's status.

The security considerations are those in CCID 3, and the memo says CCID 4 introduces no new security considerations. It assigns DCCP CCID value 4, option types 192 through 195, and feature number 192, with specified values reserved for experimental and testing use.
sections.plainLanguage: This profile is experimental, not a recommendation for widespread deployment. The memo says it adds no security considerations beyond those already associated with CCID 3.
